title.narrative: Supporting Gender Equality in Sudan Educational System

description.narrative: Context: Sudan is currently undergoing war which has resulted in complete halt to the educational system, thus adding more gravity to the already low level of literacy among girls and women. In 2012, the Illiterate Sudanese above 15 years old were estimated at the level of about 27% (about 20% of men and 35% of women), i.e. about 5.8 mln people in total including about 2.0 mln men and 3.8 mln women. According to UIS, the total literacy rate has been 75.9%and the literacy rate for males 83.3%and females 68.6%. Sudan Household Survey for 2010 indicated that for overall level of the Sudan, only 45% of young women (15-24 years) is literate, while the literacy rate among the poorest households falls to 20%. The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS)for (2014) has shown that Percentage of young women age 15-24 years who are able to read a short simple statement about everyday life or who attended secondary or higher education was 59.8. The available resources to address the issue are insufficient even to cover all Sudanese states by appropriate ToTs strengthening the non-formal education system – during 2016-17 the NCLAE and UNESCO succeeded to cover by ToTs just 4 states from 18 states in Sudan. In addition to ToTs and out-of-school teacher training, it is possible to install across Sudan the Community Learning Centers –enriching the access to different types of literacy for most vulnerable groups of Sudanese population. Programs and projects of literacy and adult education, children and youth outside the school are implemented by teachers from different levels after being exposed to good training and having access to basic training courses at Shendi center for adult education leaders. there is a clear gap in demand for schooling among some communities and families, especially with respect to girls; nevertheless, any lack in enthusiasm for schooling merely exacerbates, and is partly caused by, binding constraints of school supply, quality, and accessibility. Making community initiative a pre-condition for public educational provision frustrates and further disadvantages those individuals from communities with low overall enthusiasm for schooling who do crave for educational opportunities. It is difficult to see how any increase in supply over current levels would fail to meet sufficient corresponding demand to make it worthwhile, with a few notable exceptions (cf. the question of schooling for nomadic populations). In the most traditional communities, objections or at best indifference to girls’ schooling remain widespread, including even at the level of basic schooling. Early marriage is a common custom in some regions, according to mission interviews with stakeholders, who also point out, however, that it is not necessarily motivated only by tradition, but partly driven by economic circumstance. That is why the report recommends to "Address obstacles facing girls and other vulnerable groups", to do so education must come to the girls rather than they go to it. The UNESCO Policy Review report recommends that "Integrate NFE for primary-school age children within the strategy for formal basic schooling (“Community Schools”)", this recommendation is very important as communities with hi9gh rates of illiteracy are usually at rural areas. The report also states that "The existing curriculum and guidelines for literacy classes do already encourage the integration of some “life skills” and/or livelihoods content into literacy programmes. Unfortunately, field interviews with both instructors and participants suggest that core literacy instruction tends to fill the time available, and that supplementary content is rarely delivered in a systematic fashion. In addition to time constraints, heterogeneity among the participants and their needs, as well as a lack of training in creating responsive and locally-appropriate supplementary teaching inputs act as hindrances. In addition, there is little evidence of successful integration in the other direction, in other words: of selective, focused literacy components being integrated (in fact or even in theory) by other actors in health interventions, for instance. Mission interviews with non-education-specific external agencies suggest that this is partly a matter of awareness, and reluctance and lack of capacity to create such literacy components in-house." and then recommends that successful cross-sectoral integration of literacy programming is likely to be crucial to reaching a larger number of illiterate adults, given that even participants who do manage to attend literacy classes who were interviewed consistently stated that a main challenge for them was that class attendance partly stood in competition to their other activities. The report recommends "Cross-sectoral integration with livelihoods, health, and anti-poverty interventions" to address this issue. UNESCO Khartoum has worked closely with the National Commission of UNESCO, National Council for Literacy and Adult Education, the federal and state ministries of education and the ministry of Security and Social Welfare to introduce and promote the Community Learning Centers with the support of Beirut Regional office. I n C40, 2 villages were targeted: Khairo Bara and ElHusonat in Omsayala administrative unit, Bara locality, North Kordufan state, 5 women associations were created and 152 women were trained in leather tanning and production. In addition 20 additional CLCs were created through an XB project with the ILO in North Kordufan and White Nile states, 40 facilitators were trained in these new CLCs, Goat and Sheep Breading courses were developed including ToT, Teacher Guide, Student handbook. Outcome N° 1: Women learners in the rural communities are equipped with relevant skills to meet individual, labour market and societal demands through literacy, TVET, STEM and higher education Output N°1: Sudan Community Learning Centres and Educational System in Sudan enhanced with TVET skills for rural women. Activities: Act. 1 120 Rural women have their literacy and TVET skills enhanced in Rural Eastern Sudan through 2 pilot of Community Learning Centers established in Red Sea state. Act. 2 15 National Experts and Education officials in Red Sea state has their capacities built in Literacy adult programs for rural women and CLCs monitoring and evaluation. Act. 3: The existing 22 CLCs are further evaluated, assessing the impact of the war and lessons learned are shared with the MoE and NCLAE. Rational and implementation: To achieve the required outcome, this work plan proposes to approach the issue in two directions. The first through sharing the lessons learned so far from Sudan experience working in Adult Education and TVET skills as well as from the region with the support of Cairo office. The second approach where UNESCO continue to develop additional TVET skills for adult education CLCs, enhancing the capacity of both adult education professionals and Vocational skill developers on how to work with rural communities in Sudan. The intension is to focus on Green TVET skills for Women in Sudan in particularly in fisheries. This will be achieved in close consultation and participation of rural communities, NGOs, INGOs, UNCT and national experts and certainly government officials from relevant entities. UNESCO Khartoum office will lease and coordinate with all national and international partners as well as with the CLCs communities. The office will also work towards engaging private sector working in rural areas covered by the project. Deliverables: 120 women have gained basic literacy and numeracy skills. Education officials in Red Sea state have gained the knowledge and skills in establishing and running CLCs.
